title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: PLAC — eucharist comparison fails; Vir Doctus intro
pass_a_gloss: PLAC. If the Pontiffs were saying in the words this is my body that there is not an unusual metaphor, or that the same voice is not to be taken at once properly and not properly or improperly, because a pact, Sacrament, law would not bear that, the comparison would proceed rightly, and they would not have our men as opponents. Now when from those words, and from every pact, sacrament, and law they exclude every metaphor, even one thoroughly trite and clear, what is common to them with me? Certainly I refuted them in the Examination of reasons for and against the Sacrifice of the Mass, part I, chapter xiv, page 429 and following. But it cannot be denied that by the words you shall die by death a properly so-called death was designated. Thus I defended my reasons. The Learned Man also has certain reasons of his own by which he would prove that the death which God threatened by that law is not only the death of the body but also the death of the soul, that is, the loss of original righteousness and the privation of the image of God. It is fair that those be weighed.
pass_b_english: PLAC. If the Papists said that in 'this is my body' there is no unusual metaphor, or that the same word is not to be taken both properly and improperly at once—because a covenant, sacrament, or law would not bear that—the comparison would run straight, and they would not find our men opposing them. But when they shut every metaphor out of those words and out of every covenant, sacrament, and law—even a worn, clear metaphor—what do they share with me? I answered them in my Examination of reasons for and against the Mass sacrifice, part I, chapter xiv, p. 429ff. It cannot be denied that 'you shall die the death' named death properly so called. So I defended my reasons. The learned man also has reasons of his own to prove that the death God threatened by that law is not only bodily death but also death of the soul—that is, loss of original righteousness and privation of God's image. Those reasons ought to be weighed.
source_text: PLAC. Si dicerent Pontificii in verbis hoc est corpus meum, non esse metaphoram inusitatam, aut non esse eandem vocem simul proprie & non proprie seu improprie accipiendam, quia id non ferat pactum, Sacramentum, lex, recte procederet comparatio, neque nostros haberent repugnantes. Nunc cum ab illis verbis, omnique pacto, sacramento, & lege omnem excludant metaphoram, etiam admodum tritam & perspicuam, quid est illis mecum commune? Certe eos refutavi Exam. rat. pro & contra Sacr. Missae part. I. c. xiv. pag. 429. & seqq. Negari autem non potest, quin verbis morte morieris, proprie dicta mors designata fuerit. Sic meas defendi rationes. Suas etiam quasdam habet Vir Doctus, quibus probet, mortem, quam Deus illa lege comminatus est, non tantum esse mortem corporis, verum etiam mortem animae, id est, amissionem justitiae originalis, & imaginis Dei privationem. Eas expendi par est.
